scores.note: The best physical comedy of the set: after a 1 s content settle the yank leaves her body behind and her eye flares, and the two beats teach "blue means two". But the whole board brightens in a single frame at the yank (2.13 s), and the 1 s hold is dead time on every express ride.
Smooth and clean, with a nicely lidded eye during the settle. But the yank (1.97 s) is a small lean that won't read on a TV, and Jun's head-tilt and snicker are invisible at game size.

The iris blacks out the whole board (1.4 to 2.0 s), so the ride and the corner turn happen in the dark, then it snaps open in two frames with a rolled camera whip. Hiding the board on a beat where every belted robot moves is a non-starter.

The jam, wiggle and thunk (1.3 to 1.9 s) is the most legible physical gag here, and the slot previews her destination and heading. But the slot first appears as a pale grey opaque plate (0.6 s), and the fill blooms red over the whole top of the frame (2.4 to 2.9 s): a burst, not a fill.

A dark hole in the glass grows from its spine with a hairline of her red, so the room reads where she'll stop and which way she'll face a full second early. Then comes a quiet park, a click and her own light filling the slot, with no flash and no camera move. Her glance and nudges are too small to read on a TV.

The thin red line drawing the rim is lovely, but she's already on the slot and facing east by 1.3 s, so the slow-motion "will it fit?" has nothing left to answer. A camera rise and a dip in the room's light are too much for the most common moment of the game.

The bonk on the flexing pane is fun, but a translucent second Maya fades in at (3,2) and rides north up the south leg against the chevrons (0.7 to 1.6 s): on a TV that's a ghost robot and a belt running backwards.

Cleanly built with clipping planes, but the mirror routine is an old gag played too small to read at game size, and for a second two Mayas sit on the board, one of them on (3,2), a space she never reaches.

The strongest trick of the three: the bright-edged pane really seems to swallow her and hand back an east-facing copy. But it needs a camera orbit with a dutch tilt, her name tag vanishes for half a second, and a dark crescent smudges the glass behind the pane at 1.5 s.

Good tape-transport physics, with a nose-pitch at the stop and a dashed ring as she reels back. But the overshoot is only about half a space, which on a TV reads as a wobble rather than "that's wrong!".

Turning her to face the room for a deadpan blink (1.4 to 1.9 s) is the best acting beat in the set, and the rewind and the replay are clean. The overshoot is short, though, and it shows a false state, so it can only be a rare variant.

Sports-replay grammar (freeze, letterbox, crash zoom, dutch tilt) is the kind of cliché the brief asked to avoid. A full-screen white flash at 1.37 s (the biggest brightness jump of all 15 entries) and a two-frame crash zoom break Lumen's calm.

The fish reads at once and the chevrons part around it. But it's a pale, near-opaque shape on the glass rather than inside it: its tail starts over bare floor west of the belt, the parted chevrons leave black wedges, and a dark triangle sits inside its body as it leaves (2.3 to 2.6 s).

Soft light streaming inside the belt, with her startled hop, a balanced bob, the tail flick and two little eye-lights slipping away south. It's the smoothest render in the set. At TV size it reads more as a wisp than a fish, and it starts west of the belt over bare floor.

The deepest-looking koi, with real parallax and a long-exposure arc of her swing. But the camera leans in with a roll and the room dims, and the fish is wider than the belt and lingers a full second, which is heavy even for a rare event.

winner.why: It's the only entry that makes the game state clearer than today: a slot in her own silhouette opens in the glass and tells the room where she'll stop and which way she'll face before she gets there, then pays off with a quiet, satisfying click and a fill of her own light. It's built only from Lumen's materials (darkness in glass, a hairline of the player's colour, light that fills), with no camera move, no flash and no jump at the end, so it can play on every belt ride without wearing out the room.
winner.port: Time: ship an everyday cut of about 1.5 s (2.47 s against 1.13 s today): the slot opens with the first belt beat, then the two steps, a single nudge, the click and the fill. Drop the glance and double-take, let the fill overlap the next beat, and keep the full version for a robot's first ride. Lookahead: scene.js gets beats one at a time (host.js calls arena.playBeat per beat), so the engine should put the final belt position and heading on the express beat, or the slot should open on the second beat only. Never read as a pit: a dark hole is Lumen's pit language and the Cube's slot is square, so the rim and notch must be lit from the first frame. Show one slot per moving robot, and none for a blocked robot or one carried off the board or into a pit. Build the distance field once per form at load. Make sure the 0.065 sink doesn't clip her ring, glow pool or trail. Cut Jun's look-down.

runner_up.why: It's the surprise of the set and the most Lumen: something living in the board's light, soft and drawn inside the belt with the chevrons parting over it, carries her two spaces, flicks her round the bend and slips away. As a rare variant on top of the everyday shape sorter, it makes every belt ride a possible "did you see that?!", and it renders with no flash, no camera move and no snap.
runner_up.port: Keep it rare: about one ride in fifteen, never twice in a row, never in a busy multi-robot belt beat. Its path must run only along belt cells; here it starts over bare floor west of the belt and its tail wisps spill past the belt's edges at the bend. Make the fish read at game size with a clearer head and body mass, and slow the exit slightly so the two eye-lights register. It merges the express and all-belts beats into one glide, so it needs both beats up front (the same lookahead as the winner). The parting chevrons follow a 12-point spine that has to follow any belt path, curves and both corner directions included, and the swap back to the stock belt material must be invisible. It takes about 2.4 s, so it can't share a ride with the shape sorter: pick one per ride.
